title: WHAT IF YOU COULD FEEL EVERYONE'S PAIN?

segments.line: So... is this just a superpower? Or could it actually happen?
Here's the wild part. A version of it is real.
When you watch someone get touched, or get hurt, parts of your brain that handle your own body light up too.
Scientists see it in brain scans.
Your brain quietly runs a tiny simulation of what the other person is feeling.
That's probably why you flinch when someone in a video gets hit.
Why you grab your own knee when a player goes down.
For most people, the simulation stays quiet. A wince. A shiver. Then it's gone.
But for some people, it doesn't stay quiet.
It's called mirror- touch synesthesia.
People who have it don't just imagine the touch. They feel it on their own skin.
In one study, researchers in Britain
tested 567 people.
Nine of them had it. That's about 1. 6 percent.
Roughly one person in sixty. One in sixty.
That could be someone in your class. Someone on your bus. Someone at your job.
Many of them say it makes crowds exhausting.
Violent movies? Forget it.
But a lot of them also say something else.
It makes them really good at understanding people.
Back to you. Your doctor runs every test.
Bloodwork. Reflexes. A brain scan.
Everything looks normal."
You're healthy," she says." Honestly? You might just be... wired a little differently."
Then she bumps her hand on the exam table. Just a tiny knock.
And before she says a word... you're rubbing your knuckle. Same spot.
She stares at you."
Do that again."
